Standard Text: Explain the founding and development of Jamestown as the first permanent English colony, its early struggles, the economic and political structure, and role of the Powhatan people.
Chart Title: Growth of the Virginia Colony, 1610-1780
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing the estimated population of the Virginia colony climbing from a few hundred settlers around 1610 to several hundred thousand by 1780.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series Z 1-19 (Estimated population of American Colonies: Virginia)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series Z 1-19.
Build Note: Grounds Jamestown's early struggles vs. later stability in real colonial population estimates. Y-axis best shown on a log scale to reveal early survival crisis.

Standard Text: Locate and identify the Thirteen Colonies, and describe how their location and geographic features influenced regional economic development.
Chart Title: Population of the Thirteen Colonies by Region, 1650-1770
What the Chart Shows: Stacked bar chart of colonial population at 1650, 1700, 1750, and 1770, grouped into New England, Middle, and Southern colonies.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series Z 1-19 (Estimated population of the American Colonies, by colony)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series Z 1-19.
Build Note: Regroup the per-colony Z-series into New England / Middle / Southern to connect geography to regional economic development.

Standard Text: Identify the origins and development of slavery in the colonies, overt and passive resistance to enslavement, and the Middle Passage.
Chart Title: Volume of the Transatlantic Slave Trade by Decade, 1601-1800
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart of the estimated number of enslaved Africans embarked on transatlantic voyages per decade from 1601 to 1800, peaking in the 18th century.
Data Source: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database — captives embarked, aggregated by decade (Estimates dashboard)
Data Rights: CC BY — Our World in Data
Citation: Slave Voyages, Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, https://www.slavevoyages.org (accessed 2026).
Build Note: Slave Voyages is an .edu-affiliated academic dataset (Emory/Rice). Cite database and note it is estimate-based; confirm educational-use terms before redistribution.

Standard Text: Identify the origins and development of slavery in the colonies, overt and passive resistance to enslavement, and the Middle Passage.
Chart Title: Where Captives of the Middle Passage Arrived, by Region
What the Chart Shows: Horizontal bar chart comparing the estimated number of enslaved Africans disembarked in mainland North America versus the Caribbean and South America, showing North America received a small share.
Data Source: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database — captives disembarked by broad region of arrival (Mainland North America, Caribbean, Brazil, etc.)

Standard Text: Identify how westward expansion led to the statehood of Tennessee and the importance of the first state constitution (1796). (T.C.A. § 49-6-1028)
Chart Title: Tennessee Population Growth, 1790-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart of Tennessee's population at each census from 1790 to 1860, rising steeply as westward settlement accelerated after statehood in 1796.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series A 195-209 (Population of states); decennial census counts for Tennessee
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series A 195-209.
Build Note: Ties westward expansion and 1796 statehood to concrete population growth for the home-state standard.

Standard Text: Describe the development of the agrarian economy in the South, the locations of the cotton-producing states, the significance of cotton and the cotton gin, and the founding of Memphis as a center for cotton and the slave trade.
Chart Title: U.S. Cotton Production, 1790-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart of U.S. cotton production in bales from 1790 to 1860, rising sharply after the cotton gin toward roughly four million bales by 1860.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series K 550-563 (Cotton — acreage, production, and price)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series K 550-563.
Build Note: Directly supports cotton gin cause-and-effect; annotate 1793 (Whitney's gin) to show the inflection.

Standard Text: Describe the development of the agrarian economy in the South, the locations of the cotton-producing states, the significance of cotton and the cotton gin, and the founding of Memphis as a center for cotton and the slave trade.
Chart Title: Cotton as a Share of U.S. Exports, 1815-1860
What the Chart Shows: Area chart showing raw cotton's value as a share of total U.S. exports from 1815 to 1860, hovering around half of all export value.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series U 274-294 (Value of exports of selected commodities, incl. raw cotton) and total merchandise exports
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series U 274-294.
Build Note: Shows why cotton dominated the antebellum economy; Memphis as a cotton/slave-trade hub follows from this national dependence.

Standard Text: Analyze the characteristics of Southern society and its influence on the social and political conditions prior to the Civil War.
Chart Title: Enslaved Population by Southern State, 1860
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart ranking Southern states by number of enslaved people in 1860, led by Virginia, Georgia, Mississippi, Alabama, and South Carolina.
Data Source: Population of the United States in 1860 (Eighth Census), slave population tables by state
Citation: U.S. Census Office, Population of the United States in 1860: Eighth Census (Washington, DC: GPO, 1864).
Build Note: Anchors 'Southern society' in official 1860 census counts; can add enslaved share of each state's total population as a second series.

Standard Text: Identify the conditions of enslavement, and explain how slaves adapted to and resisted bondage in their daily lives, including Nat Turner's revolt.
Chart Title: Growth of the Enslaved Population in the United States, 1790-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart of the total enslaved population of the United States at each census from 1790 to 1860, rising from under 700,000 to roughly four million.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series A 91-104 (Population, by race and status: free and enslaved), decennial 1790-1860
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series A 91-104.
Build Note: After the 1808 import ban, growth reflects natural increase within the U.S. — a key point for conditions of enslavement.

Standard Text:
Explain the development of the American Industrial Revolution, including:
• Eli Whitney and interchangeable parts
• Emergence of trade unions
• Lowell System
• Role of the textile industry
• Samuel Slater
Chart Title: Rise of the U.S. Cotton Textile Industry, 1810-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart of active cotton-spinning spindles in U.S. textile mills from 1810 to 1860, climbing rapidly as the Lowell System spread.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series P 265-277 (Cotton consumed and cotton-spinning spindles in place)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series P 265-277.

Standard Text: Describe how technological developments affected the growth of the industrial economy and cities in the North.
Chart Title: Growth of Northern Cities, 1790-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart comparing the populations of New York, Philadelphia, and Boston at each census from 1790 to 1860, all rising steeply.
Data Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Population of the 100 Largest Urban Places, 1790-1990 (New York, Philadelphia, Boston)
Citation: Campbell Gibson, Population of the 100 Largest Cities and Other Urban Places in the United States: 1790 to 1990, U.S. Census Bureau Working Paper No. 27 (1998).
Build Note: Links industrial/technological growth to Northern urbanization using an official Census historical-cities table.

Standard Text: Identify the push-pull factors for Irish and German immigrants, and describe the impact of their arrival in the U.S. prior to the Civil War.
Chart Title: Irish and German Immigration to the U.S., 1820-1860
What the Chart Shows: Two-line chart of annual immigration from Ireland and from the German states, 1820-1860, both surging in the late 1840s and 1850s.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series C 89-119 (Immigrants, by country of last residence — Ireland and Germany)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series C 89-119.
Build Note: Annotate the Irish Potato Famine (1845-52) and 1848 German revolutions as push factors driving the visible spikes.

Standard Text: Analyze the development of roads, canals, railroads, and steamboats throughout the U.S., including the Erie Canal and the National Road.
Chart Title: U.S. Railroad Mileage in Operation, 1830-1860
What the Chart Shows: Line chart of total miles of railroad in operation in the United States from 1830 to 1860, rising from a few dozen miles to about 30,000.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series Q 321-328 (Railroad mileage operated)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series Q 321-328.
Build Note: Supports the transportation-revolution standard; can pair with canal mileage from the same volume.

Standard Text: Analyze the concept of Manifest Destiny and its impact on the development of the nation, and describe the economic incentives for westward expansion.
Chart Title: Territorial Growth of the United States by Acquisition
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart comparing land area in square miles added by each U.S. territorial acquisition, with the Louisiana Purchase and Mexican Cession largest.

Unit / Cluster: Expansion and Division of the Nation (1820s-1860s)
Standard Text: Explain the reasons for and the provisions of the Missouri Compromise (i.e., Compromise of 1820) and its impact on expansion.
Chart Title: Balance of Free and Slave States, 1789-1860
What the Chart Shows: Step chart tracking the running count of free versus slave states from 1789 to 1860, showing the deliberate one-for-one balance around the Missouri Compromise.
Data Source: Dates and free/slave status of state admissions (public statutory record); cross-checked with Historical Statistics population-by-state series
Data Rights: Public domain (U.S. federal government work / public record)
Citation: Compiled from U.S. state admission acts (public record) and U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (1975).
Build Note: Counts are derived from the public statutory record of admissions (not invented figures); mark 1820 Missouri/Maine and the paired admissions that followed.

Unit / Cluster: Expansion and Division of the Nation (1820s-1860s)
Standard Text: Analyze the discovery of gold in California, its social and economic impact on the U.S., and the major migratory movement (including the forty-niners and Asian immigrants).
Chart Title: U.S. Gold Production During the Rush, 1847-1860
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart of the annual value of U.S. gold production from 1847 to 1860, jumping sharply after the 1848 California discovery.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series M 270-283 (Gold production, value)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series M 270-283.

Standard Text: Describe the election of 1860 and its candidates (i.e., John Bell, Stephen Douglas, Abraham Lincoln, and John Breckinridge), and analyze how the campaigns reflected sectional turmoil in the country.
Chart Title: The Election of 1860: Popular Vote by Candidate
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart of the 1860 popular vote for Lincoln, Douglas, Breckinridge, and Bell, showing Lincoln's plurality despite a divided field.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Series Y 27-78 (Popular vote cast for President, by party — 1860: Lincoln, Douglas, Breckinridge, Bell)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Washington, DC: GPO, 1975), Series Y 27-78.

• Military strategies
• Roles of President Abraham Lincoln and Jefferson Davis
• Significance of Fort Sumter
• Geographical divisions within states
Chart Title: Union vs. Confederacy: Population in 1860
What the Chart Shows: Grouped bar chart comparing Union and Confederate 1860 populations, split into free and enslaved, showing the Union's large free-population advantage.

Standard Text: Describe African American involvement in the Union army, including the Massachusetts 54th Regiment at Fort Wagner and the 13th U.S. Colored Troops in the Battle of Nashville. (T.C.A. § 49-6-1006)

What the Chart Shows: Grouped bar chart of registered white and Black voters by former Confederate state in 1867, showing Black-registered majorities or near-majorities in several states.

What the Chart Shows: Line chart of the number of Freedmen's Bureau schools and enrolled pupils from 1865 to 1870, rising steadily as freedpeople pursued education.
Data Source: Semiannual Reports of the Superintendent of Education, Freedmen's Bureau — number of schools, teachers, and pupils, 1865-1870
Citation: Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, Semi-Annual Reports on Schools for Freedmen (Washington, DC: GPO, 1866-1870).
